prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which established the incretin principle underlying treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: I keep a single-part B027 prize crediting Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The chair is right that unanimity at opening and in round 1 can hide different readings of what is being honoured, so I state mine: the achievement is the physiology and molecular identity of GLP-1, meaning the incretin effect and proglucagon biology (Holst, Drucker) and the identity of the biologically active GLP-1(7-36)amide/(7-37) forms (Mojsov). It is not the pharmaceutical optimisation of a drug. That reading gives a coherent chain from mechanism to patient. It is independently confirmed in very large randomized outcome trials, now reaching glycaemic control, weight, and cardiovascular and renal risk. It has also opened a new view of gut-pancreas-brain signalling, so it is more than a drug story. No member recorded a maturity objection. Having read all six round-1 files, I find that the chair's and Perlmann's arguments strengthened rather than weakened this reading, because the physiology reading is the one that lets a three-name credit be defended on the science rather than on commercial visibility.
statement.case_against: The attribution problem is not resolved by round 1 and I will not pretend it is. Four credited names compete for three seats. Knudsen's long-acting analogue engineering is what turned the physiology into usable medicines, and Mojsov's priority for the active peptide relative to Habener's group, who are outside the supplied credit list, cannot be settled from the materials I am allowed to use. If the committee judged the priority question decisive, the honest choice would be to define the achievement as incretin-based therapy and move Knudsen into the third seat, which then makes Habener harder to omit. A physiology prize also risks looking as if it passes over the people who delivered the clinical effect. I accept that residual cost. Because the supplied credit list was built for the ballot rather than adjudicated, I give its silence on Habener little weight either way.

responses.point: The chair moved from an opening trio that included Knudsen to the physiology trio after hearing colleagues, and disclosed that this is not independent confirmation.
responses.response: I appreciate that disclosure, and it applies to me too. My own round-1 position did not change after hearing others, so I treat the convergence as partly independent and partly social. That is why I tested the Knudsen alternative rather than assumed it away. My answer to the chair's first question is that the Committee should define the achievement as GLP-1 physiology and active form. The proposed citation names the incretin principle and treatment as the consequence, not as the thing rewarded. Knudsen's analogue engineering is acknowledged in that wording without being credited. If a majority prefers the therapy reading, I would accept it only if the citation says so openly. I would not accept a hybrid wording that quietly credits a drug development while claiming to honour physiology.

responses.point: Sandberg proposes a physiology citation and keeps B020 (cGAS-STING) as first alternative, arguing that older and cleaner mechanistic discoveries risk being passed over for an exceptionally visible clinical story.
responses.response: That is a fair warning, and I cannot dismiss it. I came to B027 because the mechanism-to-patient chain is complete, not because of its visibility. B020 is the cleanest two-person mechanism on the list, and I do not doubt the science. My hesitation is the chair's maturity question. Without any delivered therapy, I would be rewarding mechanism alone, which the Committee can do, but I see no urgency this year. The unresolved Ishikawa, Sun and Wu claims and the cyclic dinucleotide precedent also bear on whether Chen and Barber as a pair can be defended. I would not use B020 to shrink the B027 credit and I keep it outside my alternatives. I would support it in a later year if STING-directed therapy matures.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius names B025 (CAR-T) as the strongest fallback if B027 attribution cannot be defended, as a clean concept-to-cure chain, while recording the Eshhar problem.
responses.response: I agree that B025 is the best clinical fallback and it is in my alternatives. Where I would qualify your description is 'clean'. Efficacy is mostly in haematological malignancies, and durability, toxicity and solid tumours remain open, as you and Perlmann note. The Eshhar chimeric-receptor concept sits outside June, Sadelain and Rosenberg, so even the fallback does not escape attribution risk. That matters for the chair's fallback question, because it means that setting B027 aside would not buy us a cleaner credit. I would therefore not treat attribution difficulty in B027 as a reason to abandon it, only as a reason to word the citation carefully.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranks optogenetics (B035) above CAR-T for its originality and breadth across physiology, accepting that it is a method whose clinical translation is still early.
responses.response: As a neuroscientist who works with the tools, I feel the pull of B035, and it is my first alternative. Channelrhodopsin changed how circuits are tested causally, and Nagel, Hegemann and Deisseroth form a coherent core. But the six names split between channel discovery and neuronal deployment. Any three-person set leaves out someone with a documented claim, whether Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenböck. A tool that is not yet a medicine is also a harder fit for this prize than a physiological discovery with measured patient effect. I therefore keep it as a fallback, not a partner. On the chair's third question I still do not favour a second part. Pairing B035 would reduce the B027 trio to two names, and I see no way to do that without dropping Mojsov or Drucker, which would be a worse attribution error than the one we are debating.

responses.point: Perlmann treats B027 as the most basic-science-aligned trio of Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, and ranks orexin (B004) third as a rare neuropeptide discovery with direct disease consequence.
responses.response: I agree with the first point and that is the configuration I propose. On B004 I stay where I was in round 1: the orexin-loss mechanism in narcolepsy type 1 is unusually clear, but the de Lecea, Kilduff, Yanagisawa and Sakurai attribution is hard to hold within three names and the human autoimmune aetiology is incomplete. I do not see it as a partner for B027. If the committee's reading of maturity requires a delivered clinical outcome, B004 would also rank behind B027 and B025, because the orexin antagonists treat insomnia rather than the disease that motivated the discovery.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide can be substantiated relative to Habener's group; the materials I may use do not settle it, and my recollection of the dispute is not evidence.

Whether the committee will adopt the physiology reading or the incretin-therapy reading of B027; a majority for the latter would move Knudsen into the third seat and make Habener's absence harder to defend.
Whether a prize that omits Knudsen fully reflects the route by which this discovery changed medicine, even if the citation acknowledges the therapies.
Whether the committee would, on reflection, prefer a second part despite the cost in B027 names; I lean against it but that is a judgment about attribution, not about the science of B035 or B025.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any shortlisted candidate or credited name, and I do not request recusal. My profile documents a co-authored 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann, past work with Sten Grillner and with Patrik Ernfors, and a shared Karolinska Institutet affiliation with several colleagues. None of these involves B027, B035 or B025 or any of their credited names. I have no documented tie to Drucker, Holst, Mojsov, Knudsen or Habener. As in round 1, I disclose that my neuroscience background makes me favourably disposed toward optogenetics as a tool, and I have tried not to let that affect my ranking of B035.
